slides.title: HTTP to HTTPS
slides.body:
HTTP → HTTPS: Why the Shift?
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) sends data in plain text
Anyone in between (ISP, Wi-Fi hotspot, attacker) can read or modify the data
Sensitive information (like passwords) is not safe

slides.title: TLS Handshake
slides.body:
TLS Handshake
The TLS Handshake is the process where the client and server agree on a secure way to communicate
Through this process, TLS ensures:
Ensures data is not changed during transfer
Verifies the server’s identity
Data is unreadable to outsiders
Encryption
Authentication
Integrity

slides.title: TLS Handshake – Step by Step
slides.body:
The client (browser) sends a ClientHello message to the server
Step 1 - Client Hello
Hello, I want to connect securely

slides.title: TLS Handshake – Step by Step
slides.body:
Step 1 - Client Hello
The client Hello message includes
A list of supported TLS version (e.g., TLS 1.2 or 1.3)
A list of supported cipher suites (encryption algorithms)
A random number (Client Random)

slides.title: TLS Handshake – Step by Step
slides.body:

slides.title: Cipher Suites: Tools for Secure Communication
slides.body:
Common Cipher Suites
A cipher suite is a combination of algorithms that define how data will be encrypted and transmitted securely
AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): Strong encryption used to protect sensitive data
RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman): An algorithm used to exchange secret keys between the client and server
ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral): Securely exchanges keys using mathematics for better privacy

slides.title: What is RSA?
slides.body:
Step 4 - Key Exchange
What is RSA
It is an old encryption method where the client encrypts a secret using the server’s public key, and only the server can decrypt it using its private key
RSA is one asymmetric algorithm TLS uses during handshake, This represents the earlier approach before ECDHE

slides.title: Old Way - RSA
slides.body:
Only the server, with its private key can decrypt it
Step 4 - Key Exchange
The client generates a random pre-master key
Encrypts it using the server’s public key 
(from the certificate)

slides.title: Modern way - Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE)
slides.body:
Step 4 - Key Exchange
An Interceptor/spying party who sees only the partial keys cannot compute the secret
The client and server exchange partial keys (mathematical values)
Each side combines the partial key with their own private value to compute the same shared secret

slides.title: TLS Handshake – Step By Step
slides.body:
Step 5 - Session Keys
Once the shared secret is established, both sides generate a session key
This session key is used for fast encryption (e.g., AES) for the rest of the communication

slides.body: Digital Signature

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
Introduction
A digital signature is like a tamper-proof seal on a document

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
Introduction
It proves two things
Authenticity 
The certificate was indeed issued by the CA who claims to have issued it
Integrity
The certificate hasn’t been changed since the CA signed it

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
Analogy
Think of a paper contract sealed with a wax stamp
If someone changes the text, the seal is broken
Only the trusted authority (CA) could have created the original seal

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
How a Digital Signature Works?
CA (Certificate Authority) takes the contents of the certificate, excluding the actual signature field"
Subject (example.com)

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
How a Digital Signature Works?
Computes a hash of all this data using a cryptographic hash function
Hash of data 
Cryptographic hash function
Smoothie
This process is one-way, meaning you can't reverse it to get back the original data

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
How a Digital Signature Works?
A cryptographic hash is a function that turns input data (like a file or message) into a fixed-length string of characters, called a hash
Input data
Hash

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:
How a Digital Signature Works?
CA then encrypts the hash using its private key
This Encrypted hash  =  The Digital signature

slides.title: Digital Signature
slides.body:

Certificate (with the signature attached) is sent to the client

slides.title: Certificate Chain
slides.body:
Why do we need Intermediate CAs?
Root CA private keys are extremely valuable
Root keys are kept offline, in secure vaults, and almost never used
The root CA signs one or more Intermediate CA certificates
Intermediates then take on the job of issuing and signing server certificates for millions of websites

slides.title: Certificate Chain
slides.body:

The server certificate is your college ID
The intermediate certificate is the university registrar who issued that ID
The root CA certificate is the government body that authorized the university

slides.title: HTTPS Internals
slides.body:
Introduction
Once the TLS handshake is done, both sides share a symmetric session key

slides.title: HTTPS Internals
slides.body:
Encryption
Encryption converts the HTTP message into unreadable form(e.g., GET/profile)
This ensures privacy and prevents unauthorized access

slides.title: HTTPS Internals
slides.body:
MAC (Message Authentication Code)
HTTPS ensures that data is not tampered with during transmission
This is done using a Message Authentication Code (MAC)
A MAC is like a cryptographic checksum shared by both sides

slides.title: HTTPS Internals
slides.body:
MAC (Message Authentication Code)
MAC is computed using a secret session key
Both sender and receiver can generate the same MAC
Logic
Integrity (no tampering)
Authentication (sender knows the session key)
Guarantees
MAC matches → message is genuine and unchanged
MAC mismatch → message is rejected

slides.title: HTTPS Internals
slides.body:
MAC (Message Authentication Code)
Modern TLS (1.3) uses AEAD algorithms like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 
AEAD does encryption + authentication together, so you don’t need a separate MAC
